questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Given Set Using an Arithmetic Sequence
questions.problem:
Describe the set $S={...,-4,-2,0,2,4,...}$ using a constructive definition.

*Hint: Take ${a}_{1}=2$ in the sequence that generates the elements of $S.$*

$$
2n+1
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the elements of our set

$$
…,\,-4,\,-2,\,0,\,2,\,4,\,…
$$

form a two-way infinite arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =2 \\  & =-2-(-4) \\  & =0-(-2) \\  & =2-0 \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  ${a}_{1}=2,$ the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in Z$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)\cdot d \\  & =2+(n-1)\cdot 2 \\  & =2+2n-2 \\  & =2n.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S={2n\,:\,n\in Z}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Given Set Using a Geometric Sequence
questions.problem:
Describe the set $S={2,6,18,54,...}$ using a constructive definition.

$$
\frac{2}{3}\cdot {3}^{n}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the elements of our set

$$
2,\,6,\,18,\,54,\,…
$$

form an infinite geometric sequence with a common ratio $r=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =3 \\  & =\frac{6}{2} \\  & =\frac{18}{6} \\  & =\frac{54}{18} \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in N,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {3}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {3}^{n}\cdot {3}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot {3}^{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S={\frac{2}{3}\cdot {3}^{n}\,:\,n\in N}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Set Using a Conditional Definition
questions.problem:
Describe the set $S={1,2,3,…,29}$ using a conditional definition.

$$
R
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The set $S$ contains all natural numbers less than or equal to $29.$

In other words, $S$ contains all natural numbers less than $30,$ *excluding* $30.$

Therefore, the set can be written as 

$$
S={x\in N\,:\,x<30}.
$$

**Note**: This definition is not unique. For example:

- We can write $x\in Z.$ This gives

$$
S={x\in Z\,:\,0<x<30}.
$$

- We can write $x\le 29.$ This gives

$$
S={x\in N\,:\,x\le 29},
$$

or, writing $x\in Z$ as before, we have

$$
S={x\in Z\,:1\le x\le 29}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Defining a Set Conditionally Using the Roots of a Polynomial
questions.worked_solution:
The given set contains the roots $q\in Q$ of some quadratic polynomial $p(q).$

Since the quadratic polynomial has roots ${q}_{1}=-1$ and ${q}_{2}=\frac{1}{3},$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $a=3,$ we can write the polynomial as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}p(q) & =a(q-{q}_{1})(q-{q}_{2}) \\  & =3\cdot (q-(-1))(q-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =3(q+1)(q-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =3({q}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}q-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =3{q}^{2}+2q-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can express the given set as follows:

$$
{-1,\frac{1}{3}}={q\in Q\,:\,3{q}^{2}+2q-1=0}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The given set contains the roots $q\in Q$ of some quadratic polynomial $p(q).$

Since the quadratic polynomial has roots ${q}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}$ and ${q}_{2}=3,$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $a=4,$ we can write the polynomial as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}p(q) & =a(q-{q}_{1})(q-{q}_{2}) \\  & =4\cdot (q-(-\frac{1}{2}))(q-3) \\  & =4(q+\frac{1}{2})(q-3) \\  & =4({q}^{2}-\frac{5q}{2}-\frac{3}{2}) \\  & =4{q}^{2}-10q-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can express the given set as follows:

$$
{-\frac{1}{2},3}={q\in Q\,:\,4{q}^{2}-10q-6=0}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Defining a Set Conditionally Using the Roots of a Polynomial
questions.worked_solution:
The given set contains the roots $x\in R$ of some cubic polynomial $p(x).$

Since the cubic polynomial has roots ${x}_{1}=-3,$ ${x}_{2}=-\sqrt{5},$ and ${x}_{3}=\sqrt{5},$ and the coefficient of the cubic term is $a=3,$ we can write the polynomial as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =a(x-{x}_{1})(x-{x}_{2})(x-{x}_{3}) \\  & =(3)(x-(-3))(x-(-\sqrt{5}))(x-\sqrt{5}) \\  & =3(x+3)(x+\sqrt{5})(x-\sqrt{5}) \\  & =3(x+3)({x}^{2}-\sqrt{5}x+\sqrt{5}x-(\sqrt{5})^{2}) \\  & =3(x+3)({x}^{2}-5) \\  & =3({x}^{3}-5x+3{x}^{2}-15) \\  & =3{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}-15x-45\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can express the given set as

$$
{-3,-\sqrt{5},\sqrt{5}}={x\in R\,:\,3{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}-15x-45=0}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Defining a Set Conditionally Using the Roots of a Polynomial
questions.worked_solution:
The given set contains the roots $z\in C$ of some quadratic polynomial $p(z).$

Since the quadratic polynomial has roots ${z}_{1}=1-\text{i}$ and ${z}_{2}=1+\text{i},$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $a=2,$ we can write the polynomial as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(z) & =a(z-{z}_{1})(z-{z}_{2}) \\  & =2\cdot (z-(1-\text{i}))(z-(1+\text{i})) \\  & =2\cdot ({z}^{2}-(1-\text{i})z-(1+\text{i})z+(1-\text{i})(1+\text{i})) \\  & =2\cdot ({z}^{2}-(1-\text{i}+1+\text{i})z+((1)^{2}-(\text{i})^{2})) \\  & =2\cdot ({z}^{2}-(2)z+(1+1)) \\  & =2{z}^{2}-4z+4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can express the given set as follows:

$$
{1\pm \text{i}}={z\in C\,:\,2{z}^{2}-4z+4=0}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Defining a Set Conditionally Using the Roots of a Polynomial

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Expressing a Given Set Using an Arithmetic Sequence
canonical_examples.problem:
Describe the set $S=\{... , -5, -3, -1, 1, 3, ...\}$ using a constructive definition.

*Hint: Take $a_1 = 1$ in the sequence that generates the elements of $S.$*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that the elements of our set

$$
\ldots, \quad -5, \quad -3, \quad -1, \quad 1, \quad 3, \quad \ldots
$$

form a two-way infinite arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=2{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =2 \\  & =-3-(-5) \\  & =-1-(-3) \\  & =1-(-1) \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  $a_1=1,$ the $n$th term $a_n$ of our sequence for $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)\cdot d \\  & =1+(n-1)\cdot 2 \\  & =1+2n-2 \\  & =2n-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S = \big\{2n-1 \: : \: n \in \mathbb{Z}\big\}
$$

**Watch Out!** 

The constructive definition of a set is typically not unique. 

Since the elements of $A$ are generated by a *two-way* infinite arithmetic sequence, we could have picked *any* term in our sequence as $a_1$ when determining $a_n.$ We selected $a_1 = 1$ because this led to a nice, simple expression in our constructive definition.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Expressing a Given Set Using a Geometric Sequence
canonical_examples.problem:
Describe the set $S=\left\{\ldots, -36, -6, -1, -\dfrac1{6}, -\dfrac1{36}, ...\right\}$ using a constructive definition.

*Hint: Take $a_1 = -\dfrac16$ in the sequence that generates the elements of $S.$*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that the elements of our set

$$
\ldots,\quad -36, \quad -6, \quad -1, \quad -\dfrac1{6}, \quad -\dfrac1{36}, \quad \ldots
$$

form a two-way infinite geometric sequence with a common ratio $r=\dfrac16{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\frac{1}{6} \\  & =(\frac{-6}{-36}) \\  & =(\frac{-1}{-6}) \\  & =\frac{(-\frac{1}{6})}{(-1)} \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  $a_1=-\dfrac16,$ the $n$th term $a_n$ of our sequence for $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =(-\frac{1}{6})\cdot {(\frac{1}{6})}^{n-1} \\  & =-(\frac{1}{6})\cdot {(\frac{1}{6})}^{-1}\cdot {(\frac{1}{6})}^{n} \\  & =-{(\frac{1}{6})}^{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S = \left\{-\left(\dfrac16\right)^{n} \: : \: n\in \mathbb{Z}\right\}
$$

$$

$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Defining a Set Conditionally Using the Roots of a Polynomial
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the missing coefficients $p$ and $q$ in the conditional definition of the set given below.

$$
\{\pm 3\textrm{i}\} = \Big\{z \in \mathbb{C} \: : \: 4z^2+pz+q = 0 \Big\}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The given set contains the roots $z\in\mathbb C$ of some quadratic polynomial $f(z).$

Since the quadratic polynomial has roots $z_1=-3\textrm{i}$ and $z_2=3\textrm{i},$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $a=4,$ we can write the polynomial as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(z) & =a(z-{z}_{1})(z-{z}_{2}) \\  & =4\cdot (z-(-3\text{i}))(z-(3\text{i})) \\  & =4\cdot (z+3\text{i})(z-3\text{i}) \\  & =4\cdot ({z}^{2}-(3\text{i})^{2}) \\  & =4\cdot ({z}^{2}-9{\text{i}}^{2}) \\  & =4\cdot ({z}^{2}+9) \\  & =4{z}^{2}+36\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can express the given set as follows:

$$
\{\pm 3\textrm{i}\} = \Big\{z \in \mathbb{C} \: : \: 4z^2+\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0}z+\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}36} = 0 \Big\}
$$

Finally, $p=0$ and $q=36.$
